meta.subtitle: The incretin leader compounding at 40%+ growth, priced richly but backed by a deep obesity and multi-therapeutic pipeline

analystCommentary: Eli Lilly is an exceptional growth story in large-cap pharma, and the price reflects it. Revenue rose 44.7% to $65.2B in FY25 and 48% to $23B in the second quarter, gross margin has widened every year to 83.0%, and operating margin reached 40.4% in FY25 as the incretin franchise scaled. The shares trade at 38.3x trailing earnings and 29.8x EV/EBITDA near a 52-week high of $1,292.65, so the debate is not the quality of the business but how much of the future is already paid for. We rate LLY BUY with a $1,000–$1,450 target range and a probability-weighted fair value modestly above the $1,141.32 price. The case rests on the forward math: consensus models revenue of $88.2B in FY26E and $101.8B in FY27E, which brings the forward multiple down to about 24.1x FY27E earnings — a reasonable price for 30%-plus growth if it arrives. The offsetting risks are concrete: Mounjaro and Zepbound are 65% of revenue, Medicare price negotiation reaches the portfolio in stages, and a generic filer has already applied for a tirzepatide copy. The Street is firmly positive — 25 of 30 analysts rate the stock Buy, with a $1,324.87 consensus target — but the range from $930.00 to $1,600.00 is wide, which is the honest signal that the outcome turns on execution and pricing policy, not on whether the medicines work.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Eli Lilly and Company, founded in 1876 and headquartered in Indianapolis, discovers, manufactures, and markets pharmaceuticals across cardiometabolic health, oncology, immunology, and neuroscience. Its growth is dominated by the incretin franchise — Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes and Zepbound for obesity — which management reports accounted for 65% of revenue in the six months ended June 30, 2026, alongside an established base of diabetes, cancer, autoimmune, and Alzheimer's medicines. The financial trajectory is unusual for a company this size: revenue climbed from $28.3B in FY21 to $65.2B in FY25, a 44.7% gain in the latest year, while gross margin expanded to 83.0% and net income reached $20.6B ($22.95 diluted EPS). The company is investing heavily behind the demand — a multi-site U.S. and international manufacturing build-out and steady business development — and the market has rewarded it, carrying the shares from a 52-week low of $712.05 to $1,141.32 and a market capitalization above $1T. The question for an investor is whether the growth and the pipeline justify a valuation that already discounts years of compounding.

thesis.body: Lilly's thesis is a race between two clocks. One is compounding: the obesity and diabetes market is expanding, Lilly leads it, and a next wave — oral orforglipron and injectable retatrutide — is advancing through Phase 3 to extend the franchise, with oncology, immunology, and neuroscience adding breadth. The other is the de-rating clock: at 38.3x trailing earnings the shares price sustained hypergrowth, and drug-price negotiation, generic entry, and any deceleration would compress the multiple faster than earnings can grow into it. We think the compounding clock wins over a multi-year horizon because the pipeline is deep and the forward multiple (about 24.1x FY27E) is not demanding for the growth — but the margin of safety at today's price is thin, so this is a BUY on quality, not on cheapness.

catalysts: Regulatory action on orforglipron (Foundayo) for type 2 diabetes, following its FDA approval for obesity and submissions across major markets — the oral GLP-1 opportunity at scale.
Global registrations for retatrutide after three positive Phase 3 TRIUMPH trials in obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.
Continued incretin share gains outside the U.S., where Lilly already leads and rest-of-world growth is running well ahead of the domestic market.
Manufacturing capacity coming online over the next several years, easing the supply constraint that has capped incretin volumes.
risks: Valuation: the shares trade at a rich trailing multiple near a 52-week high, so even a small growth disappointment could compress them sharply.
Concentration: Mounjaro and Zepbound are the bulk of revenue, so the whole thesis rides on two incretin brands.
Drug pricing: the Inflation Reduction Act reaches Lilly's portfolio in stages, and international reference-pricing efforts could pressure realized prices.
Generic and competitive entry: a generic maker has filed for a tirzepatide copy, and the competing Wegovy franchise remains a direct rival in obesity.

financials.incomeCommentary: The income statement is the clearest evidence of the franchise. Revenue grew from $28.3B in FY21 to $65.2B in FY25 — a 44.7% increase in the latest year alone — while gross margin widened each year from 74.2% to 83.0% on favorable product mix, and operating margin stepped up from 22.4% to 40.4% as scale outran cost. FY25 net income was $20.6B and diluted EPS $22.95. The most recent quarter extended the run: Q2'26 revenue of $23B was up 47.7% year over year at a 39.1% operating margin, and the 10-Q shows quarterly net income of $7,095M and diluted GAAP EPS of $7.94, with six-month revenue of $42,773M up 51%. Management presents the business on a non-GAAP basis — Q2 non-GAAP EPS of $8.38 (which itself included $3.03 of acquired in-process R&D charges) and an 86.3% non-GAAP gross margin — and the gap to GAAP is driven by amortization, IPR&D, and special charges; we anchor valuation on GAAP and treat the non-GAAP figures as management's operating view. Consensus looks for revenue of $88.2B in FY26E and $101.8B in FY27E, with EPS of $36.73 then $47.32 — a growth rate few companies of this size can match, and the number the price is underwriting.
financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet is sound and deliberately levered for growth. Lilly closed FY25 with $7.3B of cash and short-term investments against $42.5B of total debt, leaving net debt of $35.2B against equity of $26.5B. Short-term liquidity is comfortable, with a current ratio of 1.58. Leverage is modest against earnings: net debt to EBITDA is about 1.3x on a trailing basis, well within investment-grade range for a company generating this level of operating income. The debt has risen with the build-out — from $16.9B in FY21 — funding manufacturing capacity and business development rather than covering losses. This is a company borrowing against a growing earnings stream, not repairing a stressed one, and the leverage leaves ample room to keep investing while returning cash to shareholders.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is strong but is being consumed by investment. Operating cash flow reached $16.8B in FY25, but capital expenditure of $7.8B — up sharply as the manufacturing expansion accelerated — left free cash flow of $9.0B, a 13.8% margin and a trailing free-cash-flow yield of only 1.8% against the $1T market capitalization. Free cash flow dipped to $0.8B as recently as FY23 during the heaviest investment, a reminder that the capex cycle can swing the figure materially. The company still returns cash: FY25 dividends were $5.4B and buybacks $4.1B, and management added $1.5B of dividends and $1.6B of repurchases in the second quarter. The low free-cash-flow yield is the price of building capacity ahead of demand; it should improve as the plants ramp, but for now shareholders are paid modestly in cash and are being asked to underwrite reinvestment.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: Lilly is expensive on every trailing measure and only reasonable on the forward ones. The shares trade at 38.3x trailing earnings, 29.8x EV/EBITDA, and 12.8x sales — multiples that assume the growth continues, not that it fades. The forward picture is what supports the rating: on next-twelve-month earnings the multiple is 31.1x, and against FY27E it falls to roughly 24.1x as consensus earnings compound. A market paying 24x for earnings two years out, on a business growing revenue by more than thirty percent, is not obviously overpaying — but it is paying in full, with no discount for the pricing and competitive risks below. The Street sits on the bullish side of this: 30 analysts rate the stock Buy 25, Hold 3, Sell 2, with a consensus target of $1,324.87 and a median of $1,385.00. The width of the range — $930.00 to $1,600.00 — is the tell. It is not a disagreement about whether the drugs work; it is a disagreement about how durable the pricing and the growth are, and that is the right thing to be uncertain about here.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The franchise compounds and the pipeline delivers: orforglipron scales the oral GLP-1 market, retatrutide reaches registration across obesity and adjacent indications, international share keeps climbing, and margins hold above 40%. Earnings grow into and past the FY27E consensus, drug-pricing pressure proves manageable, and the shares re-rate toward the top of the Street's range around the $1,600 high target.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Growth is delivered roughly in line with consensus and the valuation stays full rather than expanding. Revenue rebuilds along the consensus path and margins hold, but Medicare negotiation and competition cap the multiple, so price tracks earnings and lands near the consensus target as the forward P/E normalizes.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Incretin growth decelerates or pricing bites: negotiated Medicare prices, international reference pricing, or generic and competitive entry on tirzepatide erode realized prices and volumes, and a single-brand concentration turns from a strength into a liability. The market re-prices a premium-multiple stock toward the low end of the range as the growth premium unwinds.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Probability-weighting the three cases gives a fair value of about $1,301, roughly 14% above the $1,141.32 price — the arithmetic behind a BUY, but a measured one. We weight the Base case at 45% because a strong-but-priced-in outcome is the most likely path for a company this closely followed, and split the tails toward the bull (30%) over the bear (25%): the pipeline breadth and the manufacturing investment make continued execution more probable than a stall, but the pricing and concentration risks are real enough to keep the bear case a genuine scenario rather than a formality. The $1,000–$1,450 target range brackets the Base outcome and excludes both tails, which depend on multi-year clinical and policy outcomes the next few quarters cannot settle. An investor's stance should turn less on whether the medicines succeed — they are succeeding — than on how much of that success is already in the price.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Lilly reports as a single operating segment, so the FactPack carries one consolidated line ($65.2B of FY25 revenue) rather than a product split. The economic reality behind it is a portfolio led by the incretin franchise: management reports Mounjaro and Zepbound at 65% of first-half 2026 revenue, and the two combined for $14.9B of revenue in the second quarter, contributing $6.3B of the period's growth. Around that core sits a broadening base of oncology, immunology, and neuroscience medicines that is growing quickly and beginning to diversify the revenue away from a two-drug dependence. The single-segment structure understates that breadth, but the concentration it obscures is real and central to the risk case.

moatFactors.name: Incretin franchise and scale
moatFactors.body: Lilly leads the rapidly expanding incretin category. Management puts its international incretin share near 55% and reports that roughly six of ten U.S. incretin prescriptions are for a Lilly medicine, with U.S. obesity prescriptions up 78% in the quarter. That leadership compounds: scale funds the manufacturing and the trials that extend the lead, and the brand and clinical data (Zepbound's head-to-head weight-loss advantage over Wegovy in SURMOUNT-5) reinforce it.

moatFactors.name: R&D engine and pipeline
moatFactors.body: The pipeline is the durability. Lilly has more than 40 active Phase 3 programs and advanced retatrutide, orforglipron, and multiple oncology and neuroscience assets in the quarter, and the proxy notes clinical-development speed and success rates that management describes as among the fastest in the industry. A deep, multi-therapeutic pipeline is what turns a two-drug franchise into a durable growth platform.

moatFactors.name: Manufacturing capacity
moatFactors.body: Incretin demand has outrun supply, and Lilly is spending to close the gap — a multi-billion-dollar build-out across Texas, Alabama, Virginia, and international sites. Capacity is both a moat (a barrier rivals must also fund) and a near-term drag on free cash flow; as plants ramp, the constraint eases and the cash conversion improves.

moatFactors.name: Patent and regulatory protection
moatFactors.body: Branded exclusivity underpins the pricing, but it is finite and contested: a generic maker has filed for a tirzepatide copy, and the IRA subjects selected medicines to negotiated prices over time. The moat here is real but time-limited, which is why the pipeline matters — the next products must replace the protection the current ones will eventually lose.

businessMoat.durability: Lilly's competitive position is wide and, unlike many pharma franchises, still widening. The incretin lead, the depth of the Phase 3 pipeline, the manufacturing investment, and the clinical-development track record together make the franchise durable in a way a single-blockbuster company's is not. The qualifier is that pharmaceutical moats are always racing a clock — patents expire, prices get negotiated, and competitors and generics arrive — so durability here means the ability to keep replacing protected revenue with new protected revenue. Lilly is doing exactly that today, which is why we rate the moat WIDE; the risk is not that the moat is narrow but that the price already assumes it stays wide for a very long time.

points: The obesity and diabetes market is still expanding fast, with U.S. incretin prescriptions up 31% year over year and injectable incretins driving three of four new patient starts.

The oral GLP-1 opportunity is opening: orforglipron (Foundayo) is FDA-approved for obesity and under review for type 2 diabetes across major markets, and in a head-to-head trial it beat oral semaglutide on glycemic control and weight.
Retatrutide is the next injectable step, with three positive Phase 3 TRIUMPH trials supporting registrations in obesity, sleep apnea, and osteoarthritis pain.
Non-incretin franchises are compounding — oncology, immunology, and neuroscience medicines grew 121% year over year in the quarter — diversifying the growth base.
International expansion is the near-term lever: rest-of-world revenue grew 136% in constant currency, and management frames market expansion, not share gains, as the driver from here.
Consensus embeds the outcome, modeling revenue growth of roughly 35% in FY26E and continued gains in FY27E — a return few large caps offer, but one the shares already reflect.

management.leadership: David Ricks has chaired and led Lilly since 2017, and the proxy credits his 2025 tenure with a 45% revenue increase to $65B, an 86% rise in non-GAAP EPS to $24.21, and positive data in more than 25 Phase 3 trials. Lucas Montarce has been chief financial officer since 2024, and the scientific engine is run by Dan Skovronsky as chief scientific and product officer, with Jake Van Naarden leading oncology and corporate business development and Anat Hakim as general counsel. It is a deep, tenured team executing a coherent strategy — lead the incretin market, invest ahead of demand, and refill the pipeline through internal R&D and acquisitions — and the results validate the approach. The open question is not competence but the durability of the growth they are managing.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is oriented toward growth, funded by a strong income statement and modest leverage. The priorities are, in order, reinvestment and returns: a large manufacturing build-out (facilities from $1B to $6.5B across Texas, Alabama, Virginia, and abroad), a steady stream of business development (the acquisitions of Verve, Scorpion, SiteOne, and Adverum in 2025, and Centessa, AtaiBeckley, Curevo and others since), and a growing dividend and buyback. The trade-off is visible in free cash flow, which the capex cycle has held down even as operating cash flow rose. This is deliberate — spending to capture a market while it is expanding — and the discipline shows in the return of capital continuing alongside the investment rather than being crowded out by it.
management.governance: A DEF 14A proxy was captured and grounds the governance view. It describes a Talent and Compensation Committee that ties incentive payouts to company results under a stated pay-for-performance philosophy, and documents the named executive officers and their 2025 achievements. The combined chair-and-CEO role in David Ricks is a structure some investors prefer to see split, and is worth noting, but nothing in the captured excerpt points to a governance red flag; the compensation framework and the disclosed performance linkage read as conventional for a company of this scale.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt captured here covers the compensation discussion and the named executive officers but does not quantify director or officer share ownership, so no insider-ownership percentage is asserted.

idiosyncratic: Valuation risk: at a full trailing multiple near a 52-week high, the price leaves little room for error, so even an in-line quarter that hints at deceleration could trigger a sharp de-rating.
Concentration: with Mounjaro and Zepbound at 65% of revenue, a safety signal, a supply setback, or a competitive share loss in incretins would hit the whole company, not one segment.

Drug-price negotiation: the Inflation Reduction Act has selected Jardiance (effective 2026) and Trulicity and Verzenio (effective 2028) for government-set prices, and management expects further products to be selected, steadily pressuring realized prices.

Generic and biosimilar entry: a generic maker has filed an FDA application for a tirzepatide copy, and while branded exclusivity holds for now, generic and compounded competition is a persistent threat to the core franchise.

Pipeline dependence: the durability case rests on orforglipron, retatrutide, and the broader pipeline succeeding and replacing revenue as older products face pricing controls or lose exclusivity — and drug development carries a high inherent failure rate.
risks.systemic: Lilly is exposed to the policy and macro forces reshaping global pharmaceutical pricing. U.S. efforts to align domestic prices with international benchmarks, international reference pricing, and payer and pharmacy-benefit-manager negotiation all press on the realized prices that underpin the margins, and the company itself flags the uncertain outcome of its voluntary pricing agreements with the U.S. government. As a global manufacturer it also faces tariff and trade risk — pharmaceuticals have been exempt from some tariffs, but those exemptions may not hold — and foreign-currency exposure against the euro, yen, and yuan that can swing results in any period. Finally, the whole sector depends on continued reimbursement and access for high-priced innovative medicines, and a broad shift in payer or political willingness to fund them would weigh on Lilly and its peers alike, though Lilly's growth and pipeline give it more room to absorb such pressure than most.

body: We rate Eli Lilly BUY with a $1,000–$1,450 target range and a probability-weighted fair value about 14% above the $1,141.32 price. This is a BUY on quality rather than on cheapness: the company leads the rapidly expanding obesity and diabetes market, is compounding revenue at 40%-plus, and is backed by a pipeline deep enough to extend the franchise well beyond its current two blockbusters. The forward multiple of roughly 24.1x FY27E earnings is a fair price for that growth, and the Street's firm Buy consensus reflects the same read.

The discipline in the call is the thin margin of safety. At 38.3x trailing earnings the shares already discount years of execution, and the risks — 65% revenue concentration in incretins, staged Medicare price negotiation, and a filed tirzepatide generic — are specific and material. We would add to the position on any valuation reset that does not impair the growth, and would grow cautious on evidence of incretin deceleration or a harsher-than-expected pricing outcome. For a long-horizon investor, Lilly is the strongest way to own the obesity and diabetes wave; the price demands that the wave keep building, and we think it will.
